# Adam Hickey

> Adam Hickey designs complex workflows and prototypes new ideas. Hands-on senior or lead product designer in Minneapolis, Minnesota, whose work is deciding what to build: which problem to solve, what good looks like, and what ships. Twenty years across visual design, interactive experiences, and enterprise software, taking new ideas from a question to something people can try: eight as a hybrid designer and developer, thirteen at RBA on enterprise products and the systems other teams built from, and now both at once, with coding agents. He brings complex workflows and operational software, seen up close; working prototypes built with coding agents; service design across every step, on screen and off (The Shortlist carries one shopping trip from a phone into a store, and his newest piece, After Send, follows one virtual payment from a buyer to a supplier and back); usability testing on real tasks, watched and measured; design systems that people and agents build from; and accessibility built in and checked on every change. Open to a senior product design role: in-house, remote, or hybrid in the Twin Cities, with a team that can hire in Minnesota.

Open to senior and lead IC roles · Remote or Twin Cities hybrid.

Contact: adam@adamhickey.com. LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/adamdhickey/

Every page is plain HTML with its content in the markup; nothing is rendered by script. Each page carries a canonical URL, an Open Graph card, and a schema.org graph (Person, ProfessionalService, WebSite, WebPage, Article, FAQPage, BreadcrumbList), and https://adamhickey.com/sitemap.xml lists all thirty-four pages with a last-modified date.

## How I work

[How I work](https://adamhickey.com/how-i-work.html): five parts of the job on one page, each the situation, the moves, and the account that shows it. Coding agents can build a working version in days, so the hard part is the decision on either side of the build: what should exist, and whether what was built is good enough.

- [Turn ambiguity into a decision](https://adamhickey.com/how-i-work.html#ambiguity): the problem in one sentence everyone recognizes, each call logged with the options turned down, and something concrete enough to judge. At Midwest Couriers I assumed the answer was a map, and watching the dispatchers proved it wasn't.
- [Build the system people and agents build from](https://adamhickey.com/how-i-work.html#systems): one design system across 40+ SAP apps, with checks in the release, and what each part means written down so people and agents build from the same source.
- [Decide where a person stays in charge](https://adamhickey.com/how-i-work.html#judgment): where AI acts alone and where it stops to ask, an ask that carries its evidence, a no as cheap as a yes, and a record someone can read afterward, as in Agent Review, a simulated prototype not yet tested with anyone.
- [Build to find out](https://adamhickey.com/how-i-work.html#prototypes): a working version in days with coding agents, tried by five people who do the work, and a build, kill, or park call made on what real use shows, as when Lucy Learns lost its voice commands.
- [Own an initiative end to end](https://adamhickey.com/how-i-work.html#ownership): the design owned from inside the team, research through the pull-request comments, as for eight months on the USDA-backed Nutrition Incentive Hub.

## Writing

The Shift: Product Design After the Interface is one series of twelve short lessons in four chapters, read in order. Each takes one idea from someone working on it, tests it against something Adam has built, and ends on two questions for the reader’s own team. The index is at https://adamhickey.com/writing/index.html.

The job is changing:

- [What changes when you design the task instead of the app?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/what-changes-when-you-design-the-task-instead-of-the-app.html): the unit of design moves from one app’s screens to the whole job, with agents carrying the steps between tools. Drawing on David Mahlmann’s “From UX to AX,” worked through Dispatch Cockpit, a prototype on synthetic data.
- [What is UX for when agents build the software?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/what-is-ux-for-when-agents-build-the-software.html): three jobs an AI pipeline can’t do for itself: deciding what’s worth building, judging whether it works for people, and supplying context. Drawing on Tanner Kohler at Nielsen Norman Group, worked through the dispatch case study and how Adam tests.
- [How do you write design quality down so an agent can use it?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/how-do-you-write-design-quality-down-so-an-agent-can-use-it.html): quality lives in three places an agent can read: a design system that says why, checks on every change, and a definition of done written first. Drawing on Dmitry Sergushkin, worked through this site’s checks.

Inside the agent:

- [What is an AI agent actually made of, besides the model?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/what-is-an-ai-agent-actually-made-of.html): a model plus retrieval, connections, skills, and a loop, each a design decision, the most important being when it stops. Drawing on Harish Kumar, worked through Agent Review’s simulated runs.
- [What should you never do when building an agent?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/what-should-you-never-do-when-building-an-agent.html): never trust a success the agent reports about itself; Alistair Greenwood’s 21 rules read as four design questions: control, proof, memory, and stopping. Worked through After Send, a concept on simulated data.
- [Why does designing with AI feel slower than it should?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/why-does-designing-with-ai-feel-slower-than-it-should.html): ten common frustrations trace to three gaps: context, delegation, and AI literacy. Drawing on Devansh Tank, worked through After Send and this site.

Designing the product:

- [What does a requirements doc need once the product is AI?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/what-does-a-requirements-doc-need-once-the-product-is-ai.html): everything a good PRD has, plus an evaluation plan with typical, edge, and negative cases, written before the first prompt. Drawing on a template shared by Moe Ali of Product Faculty.
- [How do you run a design sprint for an AI product?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/how-do-you-run-a-design-sprint-for-an-ai-product.html): keep the five days and add data, the AI’s role, its autonomy boundary, and trust; test the wrong answer too. Drawing on Bansi Mehta’s workbook, worked through Dispatch Cockpit.
- [Why didn’t more AI answers bring more clarity?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/why-didnt-more-ai-answers-bring-more-clarity.html): gathering got cheap and making sense didn’t; end a round of research on purpose and decide. Drawing on Ramya Anand, worked through Agent Review’s simulated story.

In practice:

- [Who sets the rules when research uses digital twins?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/who-sets-the-rules-when-research-uses-digital-twins.html): researchers, once, before deadline pressure: a twin can answer what people said, only people what is true now. Drawing on Vivek Srivastava and Nielsen Norman Group’s research on synthetic users.
- [What makes onboarding in an AI app feel personal?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/what-makes-onboarding-in-an-ai-app-feel-personal.html): ask only what the AI will use, about real constraints, and build the result in front of the person. Drawing on Josim Uddin’s Nutry, worked through Lucy Learns.
- [What comes first when you redesign an AI product?](https://adamhickey.com/writing/what-should-come-first-when-you-redesign-an-ai-product.html): cut complexity, then rethink the core patterns, then refresh the surface. Drawing on Chris Halaska’s YouSpot redesign, worked through Agent Review.

## Case studies

- [Making 40+ enterprise apps feel like one product](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/sap-product-maturity.html): lead UX for a global food and agriculture company's SAP Fiori suite, 40+ apps built by different teams with their own product owners: audits walked through app by app, one design system with an accessibility standard, checks in the release process, and a product-health scorecard each team ran itself, so it held after he left. UI defects in production roughly halved, about a third less time from design to development, and NPS up about 20 points over several releases.
- [Where a person checks an agent before it reaches SAP](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/agentic-sto-approval.html): UX design consultant for the same company's supply chain team, who found the account-lock risk by asking engineering what happens when SAP says no, designed the three kinds of flag, and built the screens from his own design system: the human review step for an AI agent that drafts stock transport orders from email before they reach SAP. Designed around the cost of a failure (the agent's SAP service account locks after a few failed attempts), with three kinds of flag (validation against master data blocks approval, low confidence asks for a check, merged lines are marked), fixed reject reasons, and SAP errors kept word for word. Built from a design system he made in code with Claude Code and synced to Figma through the Figma MCP server. The review screen is a Microsoft Power App, and the design was approved in the second review and is being built.
- [Grant tools unified into a platform people trust](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/usda-operational-overhead.html): lead UX design consultant for the USDA-backed Nutrition Incentive Hub: interviews, journey maps, and a system audit, a service map of who touches a grant before and after, one record carrying each grant from application through review, reporting, and analysis so each role starts from what the last one produced, one portal and Power BI platform, and a 45-to-55-hour analysis request brought to just over ten.
- [A brand and platform for a global innovation network](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/innovators-studio-visual-identity.html): identity, illustration, and badges, a template library, and a SharePoint portal (community hub, innovators directory, learning path) for a worldwide innovation network over four fiscal years, led with a creative director and a production designer he mentored; campaign production time roughly halved.
- [13 years designing enterprise software](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/enterprise-consulting.html): the RBA years, 2013 to 2026, for CBRE, Toro, Banner Bank, and International Trucks.
- [8 years as a hybrid designer / developer](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/hybrid-designer.html): three Minneapolis studios, 2005 to 2013, the last five years at Pixel Farm.
- [One real-time view of a 450+ truck fleet](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/dispatch-complexity.html): lead product design for Midwest Couriers, a research-led dispatch cockpit.

## Built end to end

Products designed, built, and illustrated alone.

- [How I built Door County Found](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/door-county-found.html): a curated travel guide with a hand-made identity in the spirit of midcentury resort ephemera, where every place answers the same questions and my sister keeps it current through a web form. The guide itself is live at https://doorcountyfound.com.
- [How I built Lucy Learns](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/lucy-learns.html): a dog-training app that works offline, built for one household, told as three tries at its session screen: voice commands that the dog heard as hers, a timer that broke on the pauses of real sessions, and a teleprompter that is the next version and not yet built. The app itself is live at https://adamdhickey-collab.github.io/lucy-learns/, and the write-up embeds it at a phone's width.
- [How I'm building Faunaform](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/faunaform.html): a screen-print studio for Minnesota wildlife art, in progress: seven animals, each drawn for one hour of one day, to be printed by hand in four flat inks. An AI image model draws from written briefs, studio software built with Claude Code makes every drawing printable (exact inks, every shape too thin for a screen marked at six inches, curves, film-ready screens), and every call about the art is his. The seven prints simulated on paper, the black bear from its fifth leg to its four screens, and the illustrated manual for the bench, its drawings checked like a prototype. Nothing is printed yet, and the page says which pictures are simulations.
- [How I built While We're Here](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/while-were-here.html): a 300mm square hardcover of eight essays, paced spread by spread, now a complete draft.
- [How I built this site](https://adamhickey.com/case-study/this-site.html): twenty-eight pages of plain HTML with no framework and no build step, three token files under four normative specs, and twelve checks that measure the rendered page.

## Lab

Working prototypes, and the decisions people still make: four self-directed pieces, each asking one question about an enterprise workflow, a connected service, a design system, or a live operation, and answering it with something a reader can press. Where AI is part of one, it suggests and a person decides. Built end to end, on sample, simulated, or synthetic data, and each says what it has and hasn't shown. The index is at https://adamhickey.com/lab/index.html: After Send, The Shortlist, Agent Review, and the dispatch cockpit, listed below as well.

- [After Send: the invoice says paid. Why is the supplier still calling?](https://adamhickey.com/lab/after-send.html): an independent commercial payments concept on simulated data, not client work and not affiliated with any bank. A supplier (a made-up packaging company) calls a made-up bakery because an invoice for 8,000 bakery boxes still shows unpaid in their records; the buyer’s system says paid because it issued a virtual card, and the supplier hasn’t charged it yet. The design problem is that "paid" hides three facts: the card was issued, the supplier charged it (the product calls this processing), and the buyer matched that charge to the invoice in the buyer’s books. One fictional invoice is followed from the buyer’s payments list (search by invoice reference or supplier, a status in plain words) to a payment record that leads with supplier processing and invoice matching as two separate facts, then what to tell the supplier on the phone (the card hasn’t been charged, who got the notice, a button to send it again) and, under it, when to follow up and when the card expires, with the activity history folded beneath; to the supplier’s notice, scoped to what a buyer would share, where the visitor simulates the supplier processing it; back to the same record, which now reads processed and ready to match, where the match is proposed side by side and confirmed without touching the processing event; and, as an alternate ending, the same payment expired unprocessed, which asks for a check for a late charge before anyone replaces it, with replacement options as information only. A stated "not processed" is dated to the record’s last read of the events. The page then shows the design work: three decisions that carry the concept (two facts rather than one status; answer the call first, then the follow-up; the supplier shown only what the buyer would share) and three in support (the invoice reference carrying the handoff; the history kept, folded; a status as words and a shape before a color), the experience architecture with where the invoice reference persists, where processing and matching part, and where each screen can fail, the same simulated events as two records (v1 a log, v2 a status summary with next-step guidance) with the specialist’s questions asked of each, a proposed study with accounts payable specialists and a supplier walkthrough that has not been run, and findings, of which there are none. Built with Claude Code; the screens, event names, and matching behavior are design assumptions, not any bank’s procedure, and a production version would need the available events and business rules checked first.
- [The Shortlist: one shopping trip, carried across phone, store, and person](https://adamhickey.com/lab/inspiration-to-aisle.html): an independent service design exploration, not client work and not affiliated with or sponsored by any retailer. How might shopping feel like one continuous experience across digital discovery, a physical store, and a person who works there? Photo search and picking up where you left off already ship in retailers' apps, so the question is what should follow the shopper into the store, so they continue a decision instead of starting over. Someone photographs a lamp at a friend's home and says what they like most about it; the phone finds four similar lamps and says why each matched, how sure it is, and how each does on that one thing; they save a shortlist and visit a store, where the phone keeps the photo, the list in walking order, and a side-by-side comparison with their preference first, says how old each shelf count is, offers ways forward when a lamp is not on the shelf, and, when they ask for help, lets them choose what an employee sees, with a fallback when nobody is free. The working prototype runs in the page's first screen, on sample data with no image search or inventory system connected. The page then sets out the opportunity, one service map drawn in HTML that joins the journey and a simplified service blueprint, six moments with today's seam and the connected version on one grid, labeled illustrative, five design decisions that keep the person in charge, each with the guess it rests on (no interviews were run and no findings are claimed), the bet in business terms, a study plan with shoppers, store staff, and engineering and what would keep, simplify, or cut the idea, and a close on the twenty years of studio and enterprise work it draws on. Built with Claude Code; not tested with shoppers yet.
- [Agent Review: where design judgment goes when coding agents join the team](https://adamhickey.com/lab/agent-review.html): a case study with a working prototype and a public Storybook, asking what a product designer does all day once a coding agent can build the interface. The prototype opens on one question: when should archiving customers in a made-up product called Relay stop and ask? The agent's plan, a review before every archive, works on a routine cleanup and on the same cleanup with one active customer added; the visitor decides whether to review every batch or only one with someone active, and sees the rule that answer leaves for the next agent, with a narrated guided tour of the same three beats. Behind it, the full prototype follows the feature through six stages, each saying what the designer does and what the agent does: Discover, where the agent summarizes the evidence and marks each line an observation, interpretation, or assumption, and its claim that archiving deletes data is contradicted by an engineering note (records are kept 90 days); Define, where the designer sets what wins when speed and safety conflict; Explore, three working archive screens built from the design system (archive then undo, confirm first naming active customers, review the batch), tried on one batch; Evaluate, where findings become requirements and the designer can choose against the agent's recommendation with a reason; Delegate, where the brief is written from those choices and the agent builds inside written boundaries, says what each check established, and stops once (for approval of a new pattern, or for judgment on what "active" means); and Learn, what was verified, what is unknown, what to measure, and a rule kept only if the designer keeps it. Two more simulated runs show the stops in detail: a small gray "Cancel subscription" link built by hand among the system's Buttons, where the agent recommends a quiet Button variant and the designer chooses, against it, an exception that ends in two weeks and a change of its own, owned by product design; and a fix in a table forty screens share, which needs the table owner's approval. Everything in the scenarios is simulated and labeled so, and none of it has been tested with users. It grew out of a real experiment: Claude Code was asked to add bulk actions to a customer table inside a React component system with tokens, stories, and twelve design rules, once with the rules and once without, and an intentionally flawed version tested whether the automated checks (a token lint, axe on every story, a viewport check, visual baselines) caught planted defects. The prototype is at https://adamdhickey-collab.github.io/agent-review/, the Storybook at https://adamdhickey-collab.github.io/agent-review/storybook/, and the source, design rules, and experiment record at https://github.com/adamdhickey-collab/agent-review.

## Prototypes

Self-directed, interactive, on synthetic data. Design work, not client work and not shipped software.

- [Dispatch Cockpit: an AI recommendation the dispatcher can check and overrule](https://adamhickey.com/prototype/dispatch-cockpit.html): human-in-the-loop AI decision support for freight dispatch, built around a hypothesis: a dispatcher spends less time reconstructing a recommendation when the interface shows what needs checking. The factors weighed with their values, where each stands and when each was last true, a close call that names its tradeoff and flags a stale figure rather than picking, outcomes on similar loads with the late ones open to inspection rather than a confidence percentage, a federal hours-of-service limit the system enforces before it scores and nothing on the screen can argue past, a one-click override of the ranking that asks why afterwards and says what it does with the answer, and the whole fleet always on screen. The interface is functional and the ranking is computed on the page; no model or dispatch system is connected. Informed by the Midwest Couriers cockpit; every figure invented, and it has not been tested with dispatchers.
- [Designing motion with Claude Code](https://adamhickey.com/lab/designing-motion.html): an exploration of motion and interaction, unlisted since 2026-10-28 and kept at its address. A three-step scroll story that sat on the homepage until 2026-10-21: as the reader scrolls, a blueprint is handed off, a tree grows every branch at once, then it is pruned and bears fruit, the argument of the position article drawn as one anime.js timeline whose playhead is the scroll position. Each step holds on a finished state; reduced motion jumps between those states, and without JavaScript the finished drawing stays.
